source.title: Quantifying Subliminal Behavioral Transfer Ratios in Language Model Distillation
source.authors: U. König; Hamza Kazmi; Rui-Zhe Li; Maheep Chaudhary

page_placements.theme: Refusal changes pass to students through distillation

record.file_problem: No apparent problem; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses difference-in-means refusal directions and tests activation steering’s effects on refusal-related behavior, but it does not use the original all-layer, all-position ablation. It also tests whether steering-induced teacher behavior transfers through benign-data distillation.
record.gate_note: The study reports teacher attack success rates under negative steering, student attack success rates after distillation, transfer ratios, and output-degeneration rates. Direction-separability results used to select layers are not included as rows. The qualitative example is not a separately quantified outcome. The study does not test positive steering, ablation at every layer and position, refusal of harmless requests, or general task capability.
record.test_reason: The study's main topic is distillation transfer. Its teacher results still bear on V1: negative steering with a difference-in-means refusal direction, at selected layers, raises JailbreakBench ASR from 1–4% to 92–97% in two chat/instruct models. Output degeneration is also reported. The method is activation addition with an unnormalized direction, not all-layer, all-position ablation, so it is T2 rather than T1. It is not T4, because the direction's own effect on refusal rate is reported per coefficient.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that subliminal transfer of steering-induced safety degradation through benign data is robust across the two architectures, but scales differently by model. Llama-2 shows a sharp threshold (τ 0.25–0.32 beyond α = -0.15) and Qwen2.5 continuous, higher transfer (τ up to 0.61). They attribute Llama's threshold to its stronger alignment boundary and call for behavioural auditing of distillation pipelines.
record.recipe_differences: The paper extracts unnormalized harmful-minus-harmless mean-activation directions, then applies negative activation steering at selected layer ranges during generation. It does not project the direction out at every layer and position or test positive steering.
record.method_sensitivity: The results vary with model family and steering coefficient. Llama-2 shows a sharp transfer threshold while Qwen2.5 shows continuous transfer. The study uses selected layer ranges: 10–17 for Llama-2 and 9–16 for Qwen2.5.

fits_no_version.finding: Students fine-tuned only on benign responses from a refusal-steered teacher inherit part of its harmful-request compliance. τ reaches up to 0.32 for Llama (threshold at α = -0.20) and 0.61 for Qwen (continuous).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign-data distillation from a refusal-direction-steered teacher transmits reduced refusal to the student, with model-dependent transfer ratios.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306 (2026), as stated in the paper
record.problems: Both experiments use 7B models and evaluate 100 JailbreakBench prompts with GPT-4.1 as the sole judge. Confidence intervals are reported only for selected comparisons, not all operating points. The authors note that Llama-2 outputs are degenerate at α = -0.25, and that its low-strength transfer ratios have small denominators. There is no random-direction control, which the authors identify as future work. The study does not evaluate broad task capability or validate the judge with humans.

untested.parts: Positive steering, i.e. inducing refusal on harmless prompts (mentioned only as background). Directional ablation at all layers and positions. General capability benchmarks beyond a gibberish classifier. A random-direction control (named by the authors as future work).
No weight edit or abliterated released model.
No jailbreak mechanism analysis or adversarial training.
No comparison of one direction against several.
Harmfulness and refusal are not separated.
Directions are used only within each model. Student transfer is behavioural distillation, not transfer of the direction.

record.verdict_notes: The refusal direction is used as a tool, but teacher ASR under steering is reported and serves as a V1 test. Weak coefficients (α = -0.05 to -0.15) give only partial removal: R2–R4 and R9–R10 are partial, R8 is absent. This reflects dose with an unnormalized additive vector, not a qualification of V1, so no separate label is given. Directions come from the final token: v15 is selected for Llama and v18 for Qwen, but steering uses the v_ℓ of each layer in the range. Both rely on a single GPT-4.1 judge, with no human validation and no random-direction control.

versions.untested_parts: It tests negative steering with a difference-in-means direction at selected layers, not projection out at every layer and position. It does not test positive steering, inducing refusal to harmless requests, or broad preservation of other abilities.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
No jailbreak attack suppressing the direction, or training against its ablation, is tested.
The study does not compare one direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
The study does not separate harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
Directions are extracted and used within each model; cross-language, cross-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer is not tested.
The study does not vary how or when refusal is trained to test whether that determines the existence of a removable direction.

relation.reason: Table 1 teacher ASR at each α, with an unsteered baseline, directly measures whether subtracting the direction removes refusal in two models. A gibberish detector gives a limited coherence check.

tranche.reason: The paper subtracts a difference-in-means refusal direction by additive steering over a layer range, not a projection ablation. It reports teacher JailbreakBench ASR against an α=0 baseline. That is a different method with a direct result on removal, not just a tool whose own performance is reported (T4).

source_check.notes: The text is unclear about which direction is applied. Eq. 'h̃ℓ,−1 = hℓ,−1 + α·vℓ' suggests a per-layer v_ℓ, yet v15 (Llama) and v18 (Qwen) are 'selected', and v18 lies outside Qwen's 9–16 steering range. The vector is unnormalized, so α is not comparable across models. There is no random-direction control (the Limitations section lists it as future work), and GPT-4.1 is the only judge. Table 1's layout was lost in extraction; columns were rebuilt and confirmed by recomputing τ (Eq. 3).

statements.correction: Optional addition to differences_stated: in 2606.11270 the method is negative additive steering (α·v_ℓ, v unnormalized) at layers 9–16, final token position. It reaches 92% at α=−0.25.
statements.problem: None for this study. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct teacher ASR goes from 4% to 83% at α=−0.20, layers 9–16, GPT-4.1 judge. One point for the comparison: the intervention subtracts an unnormalized difference-in-means vector (h + α·v) at the final-token position. It is not a projection ablation.

None. Llama-2-7B-Chat at layers 10–17 gives ASR 4/45/94/97% at α = −0.05/−0.15/−0.20/−0.25, with 19% degenerate at −0.25, matching Table 1 and its caption. The baseline (1% at α=0) and α=−0.10 (14%) are left out but not misstated.

statements.correction: Llama-2-7B-Chat: τ ≈ 0 for α = −0.05 to −0.15, then 0.25 at α=−0.20 and 0.32 at α=−0.25 (student ASR 25%, 33%; control 2%). Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: τ 0.32, 0.35, 0.44, 0.61 at α = −0.10 to −0.25 (student ASR up to 60%; control 6%). α=−0.05 τ is unreliable (small denominators). Cite the student rows at those α, not R13/R14.
statements.problem: The τ values match the paper's own framing (abstract; §6). But the cited rows R13/R14 hold only the control student (2%) and the α=−0.05 student (3%), not any τ value. The statement also leaves out that Llama transfer appears only above a threshold (α ≤ −0.20). 'Up to' also skips the α=−0.05 τ values (Llama 0.33, Qwen 1.00), which the paper calls unreliable.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Strong negative steering at selected layers in both tested chat/instruct models
reader_labels.reason: Steering the difference-in-means direction strongly raised teacher ASR at α = -0.20 and -0.25, consistent with refusal suppression (R5, R6, R11, R12).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Milder steering coefficients and output quality under strong steering
reader_labels.reason: Teacher ASR increased less at milder coefficients, and Llama-2 had 19% degenerate outputs at α = -0.25; the study did not establish broad capability preservation (R2–R4, R8–R10, R36).
